description.narrative: Intervention strategy 1: Capacity Strengthening of Local Actors in providing evidence-based Child Protection, Education and PSS programming and service deliveryIntervention Strategy 2: Direct funding for in-country partners for organizational or programmatic investments and additional learning needsIntervention strategy 3: Refugees and host communities are meaningfully engaged in decisions and actions that affect their communities

War Child will collaborate with local organizations in its approach to enhance prospects for children and youth from conflict-affected refugees and host communities. War Child follows a child rights-based approach, working alongside children, young people and their communities to better understand, acknowledge and claim their rights whilst holding duty bearers accountable. Engagement with local organizations is based on complementarity, mutual learning and expertise sharing, building on existing capabilities based on needs and interests identified by partner organizations, while providing direct financial support to make organizational and programmatic investments.

title.narrative: Sub-result area 4a. UN and IFI partners programme in a more aligned and work in complementary manner in protracted displacement
4.c Evidence of partners increasing frequency of joint-up planning, programming, and reporting (qualitative) (PROSPECTS 5 b)

comment.narrative: Across Lebanon and Uganda, joint planning, programming, monitoring, and reporting of partner activities were conducted through coordinated collaboration to ensure effective and contextually relevant implementation. In both contexts, partners worked together to review progress, share information, and align activities with programme objectives in education and social protection. Regular coordination mechanisms and learning platforms, including Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) discussions, supported reflection on implementation challenges, lessons learned, and improvements for future programming.Lebanon:In Lebanon, collaboration was primarily facilitated through close coordination between the Implementing Country Partner (ICP) and the Strategic Partner (SP). During the first year of the project, partners jointly developed the implementation plan by sharing ideas, strengthening coordination, and building partner capacity in conducting community needs assessments and analyzing results. Programming priorities were defined based on these assessments. Coordination has been maintained through daily informal communication, monthly meetings, and quarterly coordination meetings to ensure alignment and effective implementation. The Annual MEL session provided a platform for partners to reflect on challenges and share lessons learned. Additionally, on 31 October, ICPs participated in an event hosted by War Child that focused on decision-making and joint collaboration. Partners reflected on their relationship with the SP and identified opportunities to strengthen participation in decision-making as part of localization efforts. These discussions informed action plans and the development of a jointly designed Standard Operating Procedure (SoP).

title.narrative: 4.d. Evidence of joint programming by partners leading to increased efficiencies in programme delivery

comment.narrative: Across the countries, partners worked as one coordinated team through joint planning, programming, monitoring, and reporting mechanisms. Regular monthly and quarterly coordination meetings were used to review annual targets, track progress and achievements, discuss challenges, and identify lessons learned and next steps. These processes enabled partners to jointly adjust implementation plans when needed, strengthen decision-making, and reduce duplication of efforts, ultimately improving the efficient use of available resources. Continuous informal communication among partners further supported timely information sharing and rapid problem-solving.In addition, joint monitoring, evaluation, and learning processes, including the Annual Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) session, provided a platform for partners to collectively reflect on programme performance, share lessons learned, and identify improvements for future implementation. This collaborative approach strengthened coordination across stakeholders and enhanced the overall effectiveness and efficiency of programme delivery.

title.narrative: 4.e. Evidence of joint programming/policy work by partners leading to improved refugee policy frameworks in PROSPECTS countries.

comment.narrative: Across the countries, partners worked collectively to align programming with national systems in education and social protection, ensuring that refugee needs are considered within existing service delivery frameworks. Through coordinated planning and implementation, partners generated and shared evidence from community needs assessments, programme implementation, and monitoring processes, which informed engagement with relevant stakeholders and supported advocacy for more inclusive approaches to service delivery for both refugees and host communities.Joint coordination meetings and learning platforms, including the Annual Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) sessions, enabled partners to consolidate lessons learned, strengthen alignment, and identify opportunities to influence broader systems and policies. In addition, partner representation in national coordination structures—such as participation of refugee-led and national organizations in localization and policy working groups—has contributed to dialogue with government actors and other stakeholders, supporting advocacy efforts aimed at improving refugee policy frameworks and inclusion in education and social protection services..

title.narrative: OidR Result Area 2: Forcibly displaced people (FDPs) and host community members (HCMs) have improved access to (quality) basic services, preferably through inclusion in national systems.

Indicator 2.1 OidR programming contributed to the improved access of FDPs and HCMs to basic services, and specifically education, social protection and critical infrastructure – preferably through inclusion of national systems or alternatively through direct service delivery aligned with national systems. (qualitative)

comment.narrative: Across Lebanon, Uganda, and Jordan, programming contributed to improved access for Forcibly Displaced Persons (FDPs) and Host Community Members (HCMs) to essential services, particularly education and social protection. In all three countries, education interventions prioritized reaching children affected by school dropout, disrupted learning, or limited access to quality education. The Can’t Wait to Learn (CWTL) approach was implemented by in-country partners to strengthen children’s literacy and numeracy skills through remedial and non-formal education, responding to needs identified through community assessments. In Uganda, additional efforts included youth advocacy initiatives such as VoiceMore, as well as teacher support through CORE, contributing to improved socio-emotional wellbeing of teachers and stronger learning environments.Social protection interventions focused on creating age- and gender-appropriate safe spaces for children and adolescents aged 6–18, primarily through the TeamUp intervention, which promotes psychosocial wellbeing and provides structured recreational activities that support children’s emotional development. Caregiver support was further strengthened through Be There sessions, recognizing that the challenges affecting children also impact caregivers. Across the three contexts, partners strengthened case management and referral mechanisms, enabling children and families to access protection services and, in Uganda, social support such as cash transfers to support school retention. Programming also emphasized awareness raising on child protection risks, including neglect, child labour, and sexual abuse. Alignment with national child protection systems and coordination platforms was reinforced through adherence to national guidelines and active participation in child protection coordination mechanisms, while collaboration among partners improved referral pathways and access to specialized services.

title.narrative: OidR Result Area 4: Global, institutional and national level policies and practices in refugee responses allow for more effective and efficient usage of development funding.
OidR Indicator 4 . OidR programming contributed to a change in the aid ecosystem, facilitating increased, more effective and efficient usage of development funding in refugee responses (qualitative)

comment.narrative: Before the project, the aid ecosystem in Lebanon was characterized by limited direct funding to these local partners, they had limited influence on programme design and resource allocation, with less participation in coordination and decision-making processes.

OiDR programming contributed to changes in the aid ecosystem across Lebanon, Jordan, and Uganda by strengthening the role of local partners and promoting more efficient and context-driven use of resources. Through increased direct funding and capacity strengthening, partners were able to deliver services directly to refugee and host communities. In Lebanon, partners adapted rapidly to a volatile context, prioritizing flexible and needs-based responses despite disruptions of conflicts.

title.narrative: SBK Meaningful Participation
3.2 # of instances where in-country partners report (with evidence) on the successful efforts to influence programming or policies at local, national, regional and/or global levels (Participation)

comment.narrative: On 31st of October, the ICPs were also invited to an event hosted by Warchild where they were asked to reflect on decision-making and joint collaboration, among other topics, where they specified how they view their relation with the SP as it stands, and what efforts can be and to further bolster their participation in decision-making and collaboration (a part of localization) These inputs were translated into action plans made by the SP and a joint designed SoP

title.narrative: 3.1 # of in-country partners self-reporting improved participation in programming and policy-making at local, national, regional and/or global levels (Participation)

comment.narrative: Two of the Lebanon ICPs (Kalimat & Lavender Gate) expressed an improvement in their ability to influence programming or policies, and a third (Akkarouna) expressed an improvement in their ability to bring the voice of affected population into responses. One partner (Just Childhood) organization retracted their initial stance that they are capable to contribute to influence policies, and rated themselves as not currently able to do that, expressing that they have yet to engage in such influence and that they are unsure of their capacity to do that in the meantime.
